details:
**Grover's Corners, New Hampshire**
The small, ordinary town where Thornton Wilder's 1938 Pulitzer Prize-winning play takes place, starting in 1901. Professor Willard gives a "scientific account" of it, starting with its geology (he gets onto Devonian rock and fossils) and describing its people as "English brachycephalic blue-eyed stock." The Stage Manager also notes that the cornerstone of the new bank will hold copies of the local Sentinel newspaper, the New York Times, the Bible, the Constitution, and Shakespeare's plays.

**The Stage Manager**
The play's narrator, who speaks directly to the audience, comments on the town, and stops and moves the action through time. He also plays small parts, including Mr. Morgan the druggist and the minister who marries George and Emily. He dismisses the audience at intermission and ends the play with "You get a good rest, too. Good night." Wilder himself played the role on Broadway.

**Emily Webb relives her twelfth birthday**
In Act III, set in the town cemetery, Emily has died giving birth to her second child. Although Mrs. Gibbs and the other dead warn her not to, she goes back to relive one ordinary day, her twelfth birthday, and sees the milkman Howie Newsome and her family again. She finds it unbearable how little the living notice one another, says goodbye to "Mama and Papa," clocks ticking, sunflowers, food and coffee, and returns to the grave.

**"Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?"**
Emily's question to the Stage Manager after reliving her birthday, adding "every, every minute?" He answers "No. The saints and poets, maybe—they do some." It is the most quoted line of the play.

**George Gibbs**
The doctor's son, Emily's next-door neighbor and future husband, and a star baseball player at school. In Act I he asks Emily, who brags about her speech on the Louisiana Purchase, for algebra hints through the window. In Act II he gives up his plans to attend the State Agricultural School after Emily apologizes for calling him "conceited and stuck-up."

**Ice-cream sodas at Mr. Morgan's drugstore**
The scene, flashed back to in Act II, in which George and Emily realize they love each other. The Stage Manager plays Mr. Morgan and serves them strawberry ice-cream sodas made with imaginary props.

**Simon Stimson**
The alcoholic church organist and choir director, who has "seen a peck of trouble." The gossipy Mrs. Louella Soames and the other choir ladies talk about his drinking. He hangs himself and appears bitterly among the dead in Act III.

**"Blessed Be the Tie That Binds"**
The hymn that Simon Stimson's choir sings in each act, including at George and Emily's wedding and at Emily's funeral.

**No curtain, no scenery**
Wilder's stage directions open the play with "No curtain. No scenery." The stage is nearly bare: the Stage Manager sets out a few tables and chairs for the Gibbs and Webb households, and the actors mime objects such as dishes, newspapers, and the milkman's horse. Actors planted in the audience, such as a "Belligerent Man" and a "Lady in a Box," ask questions about drinking, social injustice, and culture and love of beauty.

**Howie Newsome and Bessie**
The milkman who appears in each morning scene, delivering milk to the Gibbs and Webb houses. He talks to his invisible horse Bessie ("Giddap, Bessie!"), whom the actors mime.

**Joe Crowell**
The newspaper boy who says his knee can tell when it is going to rain. The Stage Manager reveals that Joe will graduate at the top of his class at MIT and then die in France during World War I.

**The wedding of George and Emily**
The focus of Act II, "Love and Marriage." Three baseball players tease George and are sent away, and Handel's "Largo" is played. Both George and Emily panic beforehand (Emily asks "Why can't I stay for a while just like I am?") until their parents reassure them. The Stage Manager says "People are meant to go through life two by two," and Mrs. Soames gushes over the lovely wedding.

**"Daily Life" and "Love and Marriage"**
The titles the Stage Manager gives Acts I and II. He does not name Act III, saying only that the audience can guess what it is about: death and eternity.

**Wally Webb**
Emily's younger brother, whom we learn in Act III died when his appendix burst on a Boy Scout camping trip. He is buried in the town cemetery.

**Mrs. Gibbs**
George's mother, who grows heliotrope and dreams of seeing Paris because "everyone oughta see a country where they don't talk in English." She could have paid for the trip by selling her antique highboy, but never goes. In Act III she is among the dead and advises Emily not to go back.
